summary:
We built a map-based EVA planner for Mars. A planner places stops on a map and the tool routes each leg around dangerous slopes. It uses real NASA terrain: HiRISE 1 m elevation models, plus MOLA elevation where no HiRISE model exists. It then checks the plan against slope, arrival after sunset, EVA length and walk-back distance, and estimates radiation dose. A 3D rehearsal lets users walk or drive the route on 1 m HiRISE ground, with a real MOLA horizon.

The challenge asks for a map an astronaut could use on a surface walk, layering data from several NASA missions, with safety and a route in mind. Ours layers MRO HiRISE and CTX, MGS MOLA, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, Viking and Curiosity (waypoints, weather, radiation), plus NASA space-weather models. On our Gale crater test plan it caught a 19.4° grade, four arrivals after sunset and a walk-back violation before anyone set out.

This matters because the plan can be checked before the walk. Every number is NASA data, a cited source or a planner input, and the app labels its limits openly.
details:
What it does and how it works
A planner opens a map of Mars, clicks stops (start, science, rover, return) and marks each leg as walk or drive in the pressurised rover (SEV). The tool routes each leg with A* search on the finest real elevation grid available: HiRISE at 5 m for Gale crater, HiRISE at about 2 m for five landing-site areas (Jezero, Gusev, Meridiani, Elysium, Ares Vallis), and MOLA everywhere else, flagged as too coarse for EVA-scale hazards. A step costs its length times (1 + (slope/10 degrees) squared), and cells steeper than the limit are blocked. The plan gets a timeline with local solar time and sun elevation at each arrival (Mars24). Checks cover grade, arriving after sunset, EVA length and walk-back distance. Dose is the Curiosity RAD rate (0.64 mSv/day) times EVA time. A “Rehearse 3D” view then lets you walk or drive the route on 1 m HiRISE ground, with a real MOLA horizon out to 70 km. The planner works offline in demo mode.

Benefits
A planner can find a 19.4 degree grade, four arrivals after sunset and a walk-back violation on the Gale test plan before anyone sets out. It also shows the fix: start in the local morning and drive the long leg.

Intended impact
Any EVA could be checked against terrain, daylight and walk-back limits before it is flown. The workflow works at any site with a HiRISE elevation model.

Tools and technology
JavaScript (ES modules) and three.js in the browser, served by a small Node server. Python 3 with GDAL, rasterio, NumPy and SciPy for the data pipeline. 82 automated tests (node --test). AI coding assistants: Claude Code, Gemini with Google Antigravity, and Grok in Cursor. The team chose the challenge and reviewed every result.

Creativity
One plan links an orbital map, rover ground truth and a first-person rehearsal. The horizon is real MOLA terrain rather than painted mountains. We first built an immersive simulator, then rebuilt it into a planning tool where every number has a source.

Factors we considered
Validation: HiRISE was registered to 478 Curiosity waypoints (residual 2.35 m), and slope was compared with rover tilt at 176 waypoints. The correlation is weak, so the tool tells users to keep a safety margin. Slope limits come from NASA’s lunar EVA ConOps because no Mars limit is published. Walking pace and time at each stop are planner inputs, not data. Radiation is treated as a time problem, not a map layer. MOLA-only areas are flagged. Gale is a rover site, not a human landing candidate. No team member is named, because team members are minors.
